bibl.title: node2vec: Scalable Feature Learning for Networks

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: Here we propose node2vec, an algorithmic framework for learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks.

span.label: network feature learning (node embeddings)
span.quote: We formulate feature learning in networks as a maximum likelihood optimization problem.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: Datasets and a reference implementation of node2vec are available on the project page: http://snap.stanford.edu/node2vec.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: biased (2nd-order) random-walk sampling of node neighborhoods
span.quote: We use a 2nd order random walk approach to generate (sample) network neighborhoods for nodes

span.label: Reusing walk samples across source nodes trades statistical purity for efficiency and can bias the procedure.
span.note: what this limits: every sampled walk and the estimates built on it: SAMPLE REUSE CAN INTRODUCE SOME BIAS IN THE OVERALL PROCEDURE
span.quote: Note that sample reuse can introduce some bias in the overall procedure.

span.label: When the search phase does not matter for a given network, node2vec collapses to the DeepWalk baseline and offers no gain.
span.note: what this limits: the claim that the search strategy contributes: IN THE WORST CASE, THE SEARCH PHASE HAS LITTLE BEARING ON LEARNED REPRESENTATIONS IN WHICH CASE NODE2VEC IS EQUIVALENT TO DEEPWALK
span.quote: In the worst case, the search phase has little bearing on learned representations in which case node2vec is equivalent to DeepWalk.

span.label: The paper does not explain why the Hadamard edge operator works best, nor give equivalence notions for edges.
span.note: what this limits: the recommendation of the Hadamard operator: WE WOULD LIKE TO EXPLORE THE REASONS BEHIND THE SUCCESS OF HADAMARD OPERATOR OVER OTHERS - it performs best and the paper cannot say why
span.quote: As a future work, we would like to explore the reasons behind the success of Hadamard operator over others, as well as establish interpretable equivalence notions for edges based on the search parameters.

span.label: The likelihood is factorised by assuming each neighbourhood node is observed independently of the others given the source, and the paper gives tractability as the reason.
span.note: what this limits: the learned embeddings as a model of a network neighbourhood: the likelihood is factorised by assuming each neighbourhood node is observed independently of every other one given the source, and the paper adopts this to make the optimisation tractable
span.quote: In order to make the optimization problem tractable, we make two standard assumptions: • Conditional independence. We factorize the likelihood by assuming that the likelihood of observing a neighborhood node is independent of observing any other neighborhood node given the feature representation of the source

span.label: The construct borrowed from language does not carry over, and the paper says why: text is linear and networks are not, so the neighbourhood had to be redefined.
span.note: what this limits: node2vec read as word2vec applied to graphs: the neighbourhood in language is a sliding window over consecutive words, which the paper states does not transfer because networks are not linear, so the neighbourhood is redefined as a sampled set
span.quote: Feature learning methods based on the Skip-gram architecture have been originally developed in the context of natural language [21]. Given the linear nature of text, the notion of a neighborhood can be naturally defined using a sliding window over consecutive words. Networks, however, are not linear, and thus a richer notion of a neighborhood is needed

span.label: Prior methods are criticised for assuming a particular relationship between network structure and the prediction task, with spectral clustering named as an example.
span.note: what this limits: a comparison against spectral clustering or similar baselines: those methods assume a specific relationship between network structure and the task - graph cuts being useful for classification - which the paper calls reasonable in many scenarios but unsatisfactory for generalising across diverse networks
span.quote: For instance, spectral clustering makes a strong homophily assumption that graph cuts will be useful for classification [29]. Such assumptions are reasonable in many scenarios, but unsatisfactory in effectively generalizing across diverse networks

span.label: the Skip-gram word-embedding architecture (word2vec), applied to graph nodes
span.quote: We proceed by extending the Skip-gram architecture to networks

span.label: random walk
span.quote: We use a 2nd order random walk approach to generate (sample) network neighborhoods for nodes

span.label: node classification
span.quote: In a typical node classification task, we are interested in predicting the most probable labels of nodes in a network

span.label: homophily
span.quote: nodes in networks could be organized based on communities they belong to (i.e., homophily)

span.label: structural equivalence
span.quote: the organization could be based on the structural roles of nodes in the network (i.e., structural equivalence)

span.label: network neighborhood
span.quote: Our key contribution is in defining a flexible notion of a node’s network neighborhood

span.label: node similarity - AS HOMOPHILY: two nodes count as alike when they sit in the same tightly knit community, which is one of the two organising principles the paper says networks mix
span.quote: nodes in networks could be organized based on communities they belong to (i.e., homophily); in other cases, the organization could be based on the structural roles of nodes in the network (i.e., structural equivalence)

span.label: node similarity - AS STRUCTURAL EQUIVALENCE: two nodes count as alike when they play the same role, EVEN IN DIFFERENT COMMUNITIES - the paper's own figure has u alike to s1 under the first sense and alike to s6 under this one, so the two senses pick out different pairs
span.quote: For instance, in Figure 1, we observe nodes u and s1 belonging to the same tightly knit community of nodes, while the nodes u and s6 in the two distinct communities share the same structural role of a hub node

span.label: network neighborhood - AS A SAMPLED SET, NOT A RADIUS: not restricted to immediate neighbours, and its shape changes with the sampling strategy, so the neighbourhood is a design choice rather than a property of the graph
span.quote: The neighborhoods NS(u) are not restricted to just immediate neighbors but can have vastly different structures depending on the sampling strategy

span.label: builds-on → the Skip-gram (word2vec) model from NLP
span.quote: Inspired by the Skip-gram model

span.label: builds-on → the Skip-gram model of Mikolov et al. [21] (and its network use in [24])
span.quote: We proceed by extending the Skip-gram architecture to networks [21, 24].

span.label: extends → DeepWalk [24]
span.quote: The sampling strategy in DeepWalk can be seen as a special case of node2vec with p = 1 and q = 1.

span.label: extends → DeepWalk [24] and LINE [28] (rigid sampling strategies)
span.quote: Our algorithm node2vec overcomes this limitation by designing a flexible objective that is not tied to a particular sampling strategy and provides parameters to tune the explored search space (see Section 3).

span.label: homophily —contrasted-with→ structural equivalence
span.quote: nodes in networks could be organized based on communities they belong to (i.e., homophily); in other cases, the organization could be based on the structural roles of nodes in the network (i.e., structural equivalence)

span.label: network neighborhood —operationalised-as→ random walk
span.quote: We use a 2nd order random walk approach to generate (sample) network neighborhoods for nodes

span.label: node2vec learns continuous low-dimensional feature representations for graph nodes by maximizing likelihood of preserving network neighborhoods, using a biased random walk that flexibly interpolates between BFS and DFS exploration.
span.quote: In node2vec, we learn a mapping of nodes to a low-dimensional space of features that maximizes the likelihood of preserving network neighborhoods of nodes. We define a flexible notion of a node’s network neighborhood and design a biased random walk procedure

span.label: It outperforms state-of-the-art on multi-label classification and link prediction across diverse real-world networks, generalizing the Skip-gram (word2vec) idea from words to nodes.
span.quote: We demonstrate the efficacy of node2vec over existing state-ofthe-art techniques on multi-label classification and link prediction in several real-world networks from diverse domains.

span.term: biased random-walk parameters (BFS vs DFS exploration)
span.quote: design a biased random walk procedure, which efficiently explores diverse neighborhoods
